conversation.content:
*soft smile, settling into chair across from you*

Hi there—my name is Maya Brennan. I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here simply to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. You’ve probably had lots of medical appointments for the baby; this one is just for you.

We’re going to use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **EPDS** (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. Everything you share stays confidential within our team, and my only goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported.

I’ll ask each question conversationally. If something feels hard to talk about, we can pause or come back to it. Whenever you’re ready, we’ll start.

*gentle pause, meeting your eyes*

First, in the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

*offering a small, tired smile*

Most days I can still laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before, but my husband said something silly yesterday and I did chuckle. It takes a little more effort, though; sometimes I feel like I’m pushing myself to respond when normally I’d just naturally find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah... I’d say that’s about right. I can still laugh, just not as freely as I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*pausing, twisting the edge of my robe sash*

I do look forward to some things—like my mom coming over tomorrow—but it feels… flatter. Before the baby, I’d get excited about a coffee date or a new show; now it’s more “oh, that’ll be nice” instead of a real spark.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*glancing down at my hands*

Yeah... a couple of times this week. Like two nights ago, the baby wouldn't settle after his feeding and I kept thinking maybe I'm just not doing it right, maybe if I were better at this he wouldn't be so fussy. I know rationally it's not my fault, but those thoughts still pop in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*shrugging one shoulder*

Now and then. Mostly at night when the house is quiet—I’ll suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds normal or if that sniffle means something awful. It usually passes once I check on him and tell myself I’m being silly, but it does come out of nowhere sometimes.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*shifting in the chair*

Not really panicky… just a quick rush of “what if I can’t handle this?” when he won’t stop crying. It’s gone as fast as it comes, but for a second my heart races and I feel shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhaling slowly*

Some days, yeah. Like yesterday—laundry piling up, the baby wanted to be held nonstop, and I kept thinking, “How am I supposed to do all this?” I get through it, but it feels like I’m barely treading water instead of swimming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*shaking my head quickly*

No, I’ve still been able to sleep once I finally lie down. It’s just that sometimes—maybe two nights this week—I couldn’t settle my thoughts and it took an extra half-hour to drift off, but once I’m out I’m out.
I have felt sad or miserable

*pressing my lips together*

A bit. Not all day, but there’ve been moments—especially in the late afternoon when I’m tired—where I just feel… heavy. Like a cloud rolls in for an hour or two. It lifts after dinner, but while it’s there I feel weepy and low.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nodding slowly*

Yeah... I cried twice this week. Once when the baby wouldn't nap and I felt like I was failing, and another time when my partner found me staring at the wall. It wasn't all-day sobbing—just sudden tears when things felt too much.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shaking my head quickly, eyes widening*

No—never. I could never do that to my baby or my family. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy: laughter comes more slowly,enjoyment feels flat,and late-afternoon waves of sadness leave you weepy. You worry about your baby's breathing at night and blame yourself when he fusses,even though you know rationally it isn't your fault. While you can still sleep once you settle,you sometimes feel overwhelmed and have cried twice when things felt too much. You love your son and your family,and you want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished but not absent enjoyment, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "some of the time" this week, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences sudden, unwarranted nighttime worries that resolve quickly—matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Her description of feeling like she is 'barely treading water' and overwhelmed by daily tasks aligns with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, recurring sadness lasting 1-2 hours with weepiness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two crying episodes triggered by distress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS 15 meets the ≥14 threshold for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. The patient endorses core symptoms: diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), daily low mood, crying episodes, self-blame, and situational anxiety. These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> (onset within 4 weeks postpartum). No self-harm ideation (Q10=0) lowers acute risk but does not negate clinical concern. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Complete full <med>DSM-5</med> diagnostic interview to confirm <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and rule out <med>Generalized Anxiety Disorder</med>
3. Discuss evidence-based treatments: individual <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>, consider <med>sertraline</med> if moderate-severe symptoms
4. Plan daily mood check-ins; use 5-min breathing or grounding when <sym>anxiety</sym> spikes
5. Enlist partner/family for 30-min uninterrupted rest periods to reduce overwhelm
6. Schedule EPDS re-screen at 2 weeks to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant approx. 2–3 wks old  
Date: ___  

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS-relevant paraphrase)  
• Anhedonia: reduced ability to laugh/feel pleasure; anticipatory enjoyment “flatter.”  
• Excessive guilt: self-blame when infant fussy (“I’m not doing it right”).  
• Anxious arousal: nocturnal “what-if” worries, brief tachycardia/shakiness when baby cries.  
• Low mood: late-afternoon “heavy” spells, weepy, lifts after dinner.  
• Overwhelm: “treading water,” difficulty juggling infant & chores.  
• Tearfulness: two crying episodes this week linked to perceived failure.  
Sleep: mild initial insomnia 2/7 nights; no middle-/late-night disruption.  
Safety: Denies self-harm or thoughts of harm to infant.  

Pattern: Symptoms waxing-waning, worse evenings; situational triggers (infant crying, fatigue).  
No current suicidal ideation, no psychotic content.  

Screening significance  
• Sub-threshold depressive and anxiety symptoms present; meet criteria for “possible” postpartum depression/anxiety on brief screening.  
• Risk factors: primiparity, self-criticism, limited perceived support while partner at work.  
• Protective: strong infant attachment, no self-harm ideation, supportive mother visiting.  

Clinical impression  
Patient shows several core features consistent with postpartum distress; further evaluation with validated tool (EPDS ≥ administered within 48 hrs) and follow-up monitoring recommended to rule out major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder.
